**STORY:** This endpoint's internal storage is a fixed NVMe drive (WD PC SN5000S); none of the other enumerated devices are removable mass storage today. USBSTOR history, however, shows two mass-storage identities that were connected at some prior point: a "PNY USB 3.2.1 FD" flash drive and a second entry with placeholder-looking vendor/product strings ("VendorCo"/"ProductCode"). Decisively, the Removable Storage Policy, Defender Device Control (`EnableDeviceControl`, `DeviceControlDefaultEnforcement`), and BitLocker To Go Policy sections are all blank — meaning no write-blocking, execution-blocking, or encryption-mandate is configured for removable media on this host, so if either historical drive (or a future one) holds regulated data, there is no technical control preventing free read/write or unencrypted use.

**KNOWN-GOOD:** USB Root Hubs, the Intel eXtensible Host Controllers, and the USB4 Root Router are standard Windows-enumerated controller infrastructure, not devices — expected on any modern laptop. USB Composite Device `VID_5986&PID_1198` maps to Bison Electronics, a common integrated-webcam vendor — expected as a built-in peripheral. `WD PC SN5000S` under `DiskDrive` is the OEM internal boot/storage NVMe — expected as fixed, not removable, storage. A lookalike that would **not** be waved through: a DiskDrive-class entry with an unfamiliar VID/PID and placeholder strings — which is exactly the shape of the second USBSTOR entry below.

**HYPOTHESES:**
- *PNY USB 3.2.1 FD flash drive* — benign: ordinary personal/work file transfer; hostile: historical exfiltration vector for regulated data. Settling evidence: USBSTOR key LastWrite time and matching Event ID 21111/10000 mount events cross-referenced with any DLP/file-copy logs for that time window.
- *"Disk&Ven_VendorCo&Prod_ProductCode&Rev_2.00"* — benign: a cheap/generic flash drive or card reader with an unpopulated firmware descriptor (this pattern is known from some low-cost OEM controllers); hostile: a spoofed/crafted USB descriptor consistent with a BadUSB-style implant. Settling evidence: resolve the actual VID/PID via `Get-PnpDevice`/`usbview` against the USB-IF vendor registry — if it doesn't resolve to a real vendor, treat as suspicious.
- *Blank Device Control / Removable Storage / BitLocker To Go settings* — benign: policy simply never deployed to this image/role; hostile: policy was deliberately disabled to permit exfiltration. Settling evidence: GPO deployment history / Intune-Defender console assignment record and registry key modification timestamps under the DeviceControl path.

**PLAN:** 1) Cheap refutation first — run `Get-PnpDevice -Class DiskDrive,USB -PresentOnly:$false | fl *` and inspect the USBSTOR registry key timestamps plus VID/PID vendor lookup for the "VendorCo" entry, to rule out BadUSB cheaply before anything else. 2) Containment — if that VID/PID doesn't resolve to a legitimate vendor, isolate the host and pull `setupapi.dev.log` / Event IDs 2003/2010 for forensic USB history. 3) Cleanup — independent of the above, close the standing exfiltration path: enable Defender Device Control with Deny_Write/Deny_Execute enforcement, configure Removable Storage Access Policy (`RDVDenyWriteAccess`), and mandate BitLocker To Go for any removable media touching regulated data, scoped to the host's actual role.
